Title: [USA] | Amazon SDE II Process | Rejected - Discuss - LeetCode

URL Source: https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/7272101/usa-amazon-sde-ii-process-rejected-by-ma-qjsp/

Markdown Content:
Completed a process for Amazon SDE II role for NYC on an org called Special Projects. Special Projects can be thought of as Amazon's "startup incubator". VPs and Product Managers pretty much pitch ideas that could be Amazon's potential next 10 billion dollar revenue generating product. Products like Amazon Go have started off as a "Special Project" and then became a mature product

I didn't know what exactly my Special Project I was recruited for would be, so I couldn't ask very tactical questions to the interviewer. Just general stuff

1.   **No OA** - phew; Recruiter reached out and wanted to get the human facing interviews going
2.   **Recruiter Phone Screen** - vibe check with the recruiter. Make sure you study heavily on leadership principles and come with some stories about projects you're the most proud of. Talk in terms of "I" instead of too much of "we". You should be humble bragging
3.   **Technical Phone Screen** - 60 minute coding problem. DSA. 15 minutes about LPs
4.   **Onsite**

 All the interviewers were within Special Projects org

*   2 coding
*   1 problem solving
*   1 system design
*   1 behavioral round with HM (this hiring manager was not going to be my direct manager if I took the offer, but within the same org)

## Technical Phone Screen

Got asked this problem:

You are given an integer array of heights representing the heights of buildings. You start your journey from index 0 and try to progress to the end of the array. You move from index i to index i + 1

Here are the rules

*   If the current building's height >= next building's height, no ladders or bricks needed. You can "parkour" or "spiderman" your way across
*   If the current building's height < next building's height, you can use one ladder or `h[i+1] - h[i]` bricks

Find the furthest index you can get to if you use your bricks and ladders optimally

**Reflection**:

*   Interviewer was very chill. I loved this guy! We found a common interest about the US Open in our intro which happened earlier this year and that rapport carried me through the process
*   Interviewer was extremely collaborative and we spent time talking about the approach to iron it out
*   I think with a hint or two, key was to track height differences in min-heap and use ladders for big differences and save your bricks for the small ones. If you have `k` ladders and big difference, then the first `k` in the heap can be exhausted with ladder and you enqueue the next difference in, but pay in bricks
*   I was able to have a working solution hashed out, but couldn't think about the followup about using binary search to speed up the solution?

**LPs**: Tell me about a time where you faced an unanticipated blocker in a project? How did you handle it? What did you learn from this experience

## Breakdown of Onsite

Coding rounds were 45 minutes coding and 15 minutes questions related to leadership principles. Study this [article](https://leetcode.com/link/?target=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.scarletink.com%2Fp%2Finterviewing-at-amazon-leadership-principles) really well

## Coding 1

Amazon delivers packages across the country. You have a road network data represented as [start, end, weight limit]. Roads go in both directions, so for example if you had [Seattle, Spokane, 50], you can freely travel between seattle and spokane. To traverse a road, the truck must be <= weight limit

Given list of roads, a start destination, an end destination, identify the maximum permissible truck weight that would allow you to go from start destination to end destination

**Reflection:** Interviewer liked communication, but I forgot that one detail of Dijkstra's algorithm of having a dictionary to map location --> maximum weight. Been a while since I brushed up on Dijkstra's, but was able to get the queue/BFS part implemented.

**LPs** Tell me about a technically complex project you worked on? What did you learn from the experience?

## Coding 2

You are given a large list of words (10k+) words in the language. Identify all the possible valid decompositions for each word in the list. By "all possible decompositions", you only care about words in the list where you can decompose the word into sub-parts where each sub-part is a valid word in the list. Pretty much like all possible word breaks

**Reflection**

*   Had trouble with the recursion piece. Interviewer gave hint and I had trouble incorporating it

**LPs**

 Situation that requires me to dig deep into the situation to find out the root cause of problem/ticket/bug

## Problem Solving

Amazon ships a lot of packages

*   A container can contain another container or item but not both
*   Items have category, weight, color

You need to support these two requirements:

*   Identify all items in a container that have weight > 50 kg
*   Identify all items in a container where item = category AND/OR weight > 50 kg

This question wasn't too bad, but you need to ask clarifying questions to understand the parameters.

**LPs**

*   Tell me about a time you had to unblock yourself on a difficult problem?
*   Tell me about a time you stepped out of your comfort zone

## System Design

Design a system that tracks inventory levels across warehouses

Requirements:

*   Handle real time updates
*   Provide accurate inventory data for customer facing app
*   Support 1M SKUs
*   Process 100K inventory updates/minute

I sorta had 20 minutes to describe a design, so just talked and wrote and scribbled some messy diagram

## Hiring Manager Round

Pretty much grilling about LPs all throughout. Got asked predictable ones and also this one:

*   Tell me about a time where I took up something that was out of my area of responsibility

## Overall Reflection

*   Grueling process
*   Lots of rounds
*   Know your LPs really well and have very good stories that you can answer followup questions on
*   Coding questions were a mix of OOD like and standard leetcode
*   Cool team though, but did the interview for fun to keep my skill sharp
*   The best time to be interviewing is when you aren't looking for a job
